newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Prague sets tone for gloomy East European bourses.
newsitem.headline: Prague sets tone for gloomy East European bourses.

text.p: Central and east European stock markets continued in bearish mood this week with Budapest the region's only gainer and Prague taking the brunt of faltering confidence from foreign investors.
Losses to blue chip stocks, which were especially heavy in the Czech Republic, pushed the Central European Share Index (CESI) down 0.9 percent to 1,396.96.
Most of the region's bourses are closed on Friday for All Saints Day.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian share prices bottomed out on Wednesday after seven days of falls and with a modest gain on Thursday the BUX index closed 55.97 points up from the beginning of the week at 3,601.99.
"The rally which began on Wednesday faltered," said Kalman Schuszter of New York Broker Budapest.
However, traders were mostly optimistic that companies' January-September earnings reports, to be submitted to the bourse by November 15, will boost the market.
"I expect the market to rise for at least two weeks as company reports arrive," Schuszter said.
PRAGUE
Czech shares had another dismal week with several major issues moving sharply lower and less heavily capitalised stocks mostly down as well.
The PX50 fell 3.2 percent during the week to close on Thursday at 504.7.
The sharpest fallers among the major issues were Komercni Banka, which lost seven percent to 2,000, and SPT Telecom, which fell 3.9 percent to 2,879.

Dealers said the major issues were being hit by a general decline in confidence in the Czech equities market which is widely criticised for its lack of transparency and inadequate protection for minority shareholders.
Foreign investors, who normally account for around half of the trading in major issues, are particularly concrened about the situation.
WARSAW

On Wednesday and Thursday, the WIG rose 4.9-percent leaving the main market flat for the week at 13,497.9 points but analysts saw little chance of a strong early rebound on the index which has lost 14.6 percent since October 9.
"It's seems a lot of large investors have left recently, and I don't think they're going to come back immediately," said Krzysztof Rogalski, an analyst at Bank Staropolski brokerage.

The main market's biggest loser this week, construction firm Espebepe, was down 18.8 percent. Analysts said the decline was probably caused by a statement from the company's president last week that it might go bankrupt.
BUCHAREST
The Bucharest bourse, which saw a rebound on Tuesday, slipped back on Thursday, with turnover sagging to 39 million lei.
With investors in a wait-and-see mood ahead of Sunday's general elections, most shares drifted lower, sending two independent indices to year lows.
Two unofficial indices, the VAB and the BIG, fell by 1.9 percent from the previous session to 285.3 and 284.29 points respectively.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) was in gloomy mood with the SAX index falling through the 200 point level and delaers seeing little hope of a rebound in the near future.

"The market is expected to continue trading with insignificant volumes and relatively low demand over the next few weeks, which will result in the SAX hovering around its current level, or even in further decline," said Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt.
Traders said the mood on the market was partly a knock on effect from neighbouring bourses.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks ended a shortened trading week mixed on Thursday ahead of a public holiday.

Market watchers predicted most prices would continue to dip next week, although at a slower pace, with investors seen likely to hold back until the government resolves some disputed share ownership issues.
BULGARIA

No corporate issues traded on the Bulgarian stock market for the third week in a row after the Bulgarian Securities and Stock Exchange Commission (SSEC) suspended trading until companies meet new legal requirements.
Under Bulgaria's stock trading law public companies had until September 19 to submit to the SSEC a detailed report on the size and distribution of their capital and a list of their shareholders.
None of them have yet fulfilled their new obligations, the BSE said.
TIRANA
Tirana's Stock Exchange saw four transactions of 364-day treasury bills on Monday and Thursday but no state bonds changed hands, an exchange official said.
"It was a normal week," an exchange official said. "Traders concentrated on the treasury bill auction."
LJUBLJANA
In Ljubljana, share prices eased 0.1 percent to 1,192.07. Total turnover was 1.2 billion tolars ($8.7 million).
Financial consultancy Dadas was the sharpest decliner, falling 24.3 percent, while Primofin was the biggest gainer with a 66.8 percent rise.
CESI

The Central European Share Index (CESI) was modified effective October 31 to include Slovenian and Slovak stocks in addition to Hungarian, Czech and Polish. The expanded index basket now contains 73 shares against 50 previously.
